claim: The exposure of phosphatidylserine on the cell surface is catalyzed by lipid scramblases.
source: The exposure of the negatively charged lipid phosphatidylserine on the cell surface, catalyzed by lipid scramblases, is an important signal for the clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the biological process.

claim: Phosphatidylserine exposure is an important signal for the clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages.
source: The exposure of the negatively charged lipid phosphatidylserine on the cell surface, catalyzed by lipid scramblases, is an important signal for the clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established biological function.

claim: XKR9 is a member of a conserved family associated with apoptotic lipid scrambling.
source: The protein XKR9 is a member of a conserved family that has been associated with apoptotic lipid scrambling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information about XKR9.

claim: Structures of full-length and caspase-treated XKR9 from Rattus norvegicus in complex with a synthetic nanobody were determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we describe structures of full-length and caspase-treated XKR9 from Rattus norvegicus in complex with a synthetic nanobody determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the structural data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: XKR9 is a 43 kDa monomeric membrane protein.
source: The 43 kDa monomeric membrane protein can be divided into two structurally related repeats, each containing four membrane-spanning segments and a helix that is partly inserted into the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by experimental data including SEC-MALS shown in Figure 1.

claim: XKR9 can be divided into two structurally related repeats.
source: The 43 kDa monomeric membrane protein can be divided into two structurally related repeats, each containing four membrane-spanning segments and a helix that is partly inserted into the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each repeat of XKR9 contains four membrane-spanning segments.
source: The 43 kDa monomeric membrane protein can be divided into two structurally related repeats, each containing four membrane-spanning segments and a helix that is partly inserted into the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in the structural analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Each repeat of XKR9 contains a helix that is partly inserted into the lipid bilayer.
source: The 43 kDa monomeric membrane protein can be divided into two structurally related repeats, each containing four membrane-spanning segments and a helix that is partly inserted into the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the structural data showing IH1 and IH2 helices.

claim: In full-length XKR9, the C-terminus interacts with a hydrophobic pocket located at the intracellular side.
source: In the full-length protein, the C-terminus interacts with a hydrophobic pocket located at the intracellular side acting as an inhibitor of protein function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The C-terminus of full-length XKR9 acts as an inhibitor of protein function.
source: In the full-length protein, the C-terminus interacts with a hydrophobic pocket located at the intracellular side acting as an inhibitor of protein function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and inferred from the structural comparison between full-length and cleaved forms.

claim: Caspase-3 cleaves XKR9 at a specific site, releasing 16 residues of the C-terminus.
source: Cleavage by caspase-3 at a specific site releases 16 residues of the C-terminus, thus making the pocket accessible to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by mass spectrometry data and structural analysis.

claim: Caspase-3 cleavage makes the hydrophobic pocket accessible to the cytoplasm.
source: Cleavage by caspase-3 at a specific site releases 16 residues of the C-terminus, thus making the pocket accessible to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by comparing structures of full-length and cleaved XKR9 in Figure 6.

claim: The lipid distribution in the two leaflets of the plasma membrane of a eukaryotic cell is asymmetric.
source: The lipid distribution in the two leaflets of the plasma membrane of a eukaryotic cell is asymmetric with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and the anionic lipids phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphoinositol (PI) located in the inner leaflet and phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin (SM), in the outer leaflet of the bilayer (Balasubramanian and Schroit, 2003; Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to established literature.

claim: Phosphatidylethanolamine and anionic lipids (PS and PI) are located in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: The lipid distribution in the two leaflets of the plasma membrane of a eukaryotic cell is asymmetric with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and the anionic lipids phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphoinositol (PI) located in the inner leaflet and phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin (SM), in the outer leaflet of the bilayer (Balasubramanian and Schroit, 2003; Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin are located in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: The lipid distribution in the two leaflets of the plasma membrane of a eukaryotic cell is asymmetric with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and the anionic lipids phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphoinositol (PI) located in the inner leaflet and phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin (SM), in the outer leaflet of the bilayer (Balasubramanian and Schroit, 2003; Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lipid asymmetry is established and maintained by ATP-dependent active transport processes.
source: This asymmetry is established and maintained by ATP-dependent active transport processes (Leventis and Grinstein, 2010; Sebastian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lipid scramblases catalyze the bidirectional diffusion of lipids with poor specificity.
source: Asymmetry breakdown is catalyzed by lipid channels termed scramblases, which catalyze the bidirectional diffusion of lipids with poor specificity by lowering the barrier for lipid flip-flop between the two leaflets of the membrane (Brunner et al., 2016; Nagata et al., 2020; Pomorski and Menon, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Scramblases lower the barrier for lipid flip-flop between the two leaflets of the membrane.
source: Asymmetry breakdown is catalyzed by lipid channels termed scramblases, which catalyze the bidirectional diffusion of lipids with poor specificity by lowering the barrier for lipid flip-flop between the two leaflets of the membrane (Brunner et al., 2016; Nagata et al., 2020; Pomorski and Menon, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PS exposure serves as an eat-me signal for macrophages during apoptosis.
source: In case of apoptosis, PS exposure serves as an eat-me signal for macrophages, leading to the engulfment and clearance of apoptotic cells (Segawa and Nagata, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Scramblases residing at the plasma membrane are tightly regulated to prevent endogenous activity.
source: To prevent endogenous activity, which would be deleterious to cells, scramblases residing at the plasma membrane are tightly regulated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Active scramblases function by a 'credit card-like mechanism'.
source: Active scramblases are believed to function by a 'credit card-like mechanism', by offering suitable pathways for lipid headgroups to cross the hydrophobic membrane core, whereas their apolar tails reside in the membrane (Pomorski and Menon, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TMEM16 and XKR families are currently the best characterized examples of proteins that catalyze lipid scrambling.
source: Lipid scrambling is catalyzed by different proteins with the currently best characterized examples belonging to the TMEM16 and XKR families (Suzuki et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TMEM16 scramblases are activated in response to the increase of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: TMEM16 scramblases are activated in response to the increase of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about TMEM16 proteins.

claim: Fungal TMEM16 proteins contain polar membrane-spanning furrows that become exposed to the membrane upon Ca2+ binding.
source: These proteins contain polar membrane-spanning furrows of appropriate size, which are blocked in the absence of Ca2+ but become exposed to the membrane upon Ca2+ binding to offer suitable pathways for polar headgroups across the membrane, as predicted by the 'credit card mechanism'.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the mechanism of fungal TMEM16 proteins.

claim: Fungal TMEM16 proteins disturb the organization of lipids in their vicinity.
source: The fungal TMEM16 proteins were also found to disturb the organization of lipids in their vicinity, likely by destabilizing the bilayer and thus further decreasing the barrier for lipid flip-flop (Falzone et al., 2019; Kalienkova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TMEM16 scramblases are not responsible for PS exposure during apoptosis.
source: Although scramblases of the TMEM16 family have been associated with diverse processes such as blood coagulation and cell-fusion, they are not the long sought-after proteins that are responsible for the exposure of PS during apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Human XKR8 and C. elegans Ced-8 were identified as scramblases responsible for PS exposure in apoptotic cells in 2013.
source: The molecular identity of an apoptotic scramblase was first identified in 2013 when the human protein XKR8 and its Caenorhabditis elegans homolog Ced-8 were assigned as the scramblases that are responsible for PS exposure in apoptotic cells (Chen et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: XKR8 and Ced-8 are part of the evolutionarily conserved XKR family.
source: Both are part of the evolutionarily conserved XKR family of proteins related to the founding member XK1, a molecule with unknown function, which was identified to be associated with the blood-group-specific factor Kell (Calenda et al., 2006; Stanfield and Horvitz, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The human XKR family contains nine members.
source: In humans, the family contains nine members, of which three, namely the proteins XKR4, 8, and 9, were found to activate scrambling under apoptotic conditions (Suzuki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: XKR4, XKR8, and XKR9 activate scrambling under apoptotic conditions.
source: In humans, the family contains nine members, of which three, namely the proteins XKR4, 8, and 9, were found to activate scrambling under apoptotic conditions (Suzuki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The primary activating step for XKR proteins is cleavage of a C-terminal peptide by caspase-3.
source: The primary activating step is the cleavage of a C-terminal peptide by the apoptotic peptidase caspase-3 at a specific site that is found in all three proteins (Suzuki et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: XKR8 can be activated by phosphorylation.
source: Besides the irreversible action of caspases, XKR8 was also shown to be activated by phosphorylation (Sakuragi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: XKR8 associates with accessory proteins such as basigin or neuroplastin.
source: Another study has revealed the association of XKR8 with accessory proteins such as basigin or its paralog neuroplastin (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Basigin and neuroplastin are type I membrane proteins containing extracellular IG-domains.
source: Both type I membraneproteins, containing extracellular IG-domains, facilitate the targeting of XKR8 to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the properties of basigin and neuroplastin.

claim: Basigin and neuroplastin facilitate the targeting of XKR8 to the plasma membrane.
source: Both type I membraneproteins, containing extracellular IG-domains, facilitate the targeting of XKR8 to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to previous studies.

claim: Dimerization of XKR8-basigin complexes upon caspase-3 activation was claimed as an essential step underlying activation.
source: Based on the altered migration behavior on blue-native gel electrophoresis, the same study also claimed a dimerization of XKR8-basigin complexes upon caspase-3 activation as an essential step underlying activation (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Dimerization was postulated for XKR4.
source: A similar dimerization was recently postulated for XKR4 (Maruoka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: rXKR9 is 373 amino acids long.
source: The protein is 373 amino acids long and shares 76% of identical residues with its human ortholog.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the biochemical characterization of rXKR9.

claim: rXKR9 shares 76% of identical residues with its human ortholog.
source: The protein is 373 amino acids long and shares 76% of identical residues with its human ortholog.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the biochemical characterization of rXKR9.

claim: rXKR9 elutes as a monodisperse peak on gel-filtration corresponding to a monomer.
source: Following its expression in suspension culture of HEK293S GnTI− cells, purification in the detergent lauryl-maltose-neopentyl-glycol (LMNG), and removal of the N-terminal tag used for affinity purification, we found rXKR9 to elute as monodisperse peak on gel-filtration with an elution volume corresponding to a monomer (Figure 1A), which was subsequently quantified by multi-angle light scattering (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Caspase-3 treatment results in complete cleavage of the C-terminus of rXKR9.
source: We have investigated protein digestion after incubation with caspase-3 in detergent solution and found complete cleavage of the C-terminus resulting in the predicted reduction of the molecular weight as confirmed by mass spectrometry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and confirmed by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Caspase-cleaved rXKR9 elutes as a monomer.
source: As full-length rXKR9, the truncated protein elutes as a monomer and we did not find strong evidence of dimerization in detergent solution (Figure 1B), which was independently suggested for an XKR8-basigin complex (Suzuki et al., 2016) and for XKR4 upon caspase activation (Maruoka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No strong evidence of dimerization was found for rXKR9 in detergent solution after caspase treatment.
source: As full-length rXKR9, the truncated protein elutes as a monomer and we did not find strong evidence of dimerization in detergent solution (Figure 1B), which was independently suggested for an XKR8-basigin complex (Suzuki et al., 2016) and for XKR4 upon caspase activation (Maruoka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No strong evidence of scrambling activity was found for rXKR9 in liposome-based assays irrespective of C-terminus cleavage.
source: In our liposome-based assays, we did not find strong evidence of scrambling activity irrespective of the cleavage of the C-terminus (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), thus suggesting that the protein does not promote lipid scrambling under the applied conditions, which might be the consequence of the lack of an essential factor required for the protein to be active.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: rXKR9 may not promote lipid scrambling under the applied conditions due to the lack of an essential factor.
source: In our liposome-based assays, we did not find strong evidence of scrambling activity irrespective of the cleavage of the C-terminus (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), thus suggesting that the protein does not promote lipid scrambling under the applied conditions, which might be the consequence of the lack of an essential factor required for the protein to be active.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a possible explanation for the lack of observed activity.

claim: hXKR8 forms a complex with basigin.
source: Whereas in case of hXKR8, we find robust complex formation with basigin, which is also manifested in a low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 1E,F) and in a recently determined structure of the complex at high resolution (Sakuragi et al., 2021), we do not find evidence for the formation of a similar complex with rXKR9 (Figure 1G), thus refuting the assumption that basigin might be an essential interaction partner of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1E,F and a citation.

claim: No evidence was found for the formation of a complex between rXKR9 and basigin.
source: Whereas in case of hXKR8, we find robust complex formation with basigin, which is also manifested in a low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 1E,F) and in a recently determined structure of the complex at high resolution (Sakuragi et al., 2021), we do not find evidence for the formation of a similar complex with rXKR9 (Figure 1G), thus refuting the assumption that basigin might be an essential interaction partner of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Basigin is not an essential interaction partner of rXKR9.
source: Whereas in case of hXKR8, we find robust complex formation with basigin, which is also manifested in a low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction (Figure 1E,F) and in a recently determined structure of the complex at high resolution (Sakuragi et al., 2021), we do not find evidence for the formation of a similar complex with rXKR9 (Figure 1G), thus refuting the assumption that basigin might be an essential interaction partner of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the experimental data.

claim: The cryo-EM map of full-length rXKR9 extends to 3.66 Å resolution.
source: The resulting maps, which extend to 3.66 Å for full-length and 4.3 Å for the cleaved protein, were of high quality and allowed in each case the interpretation with an atomic model (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and documented in Table 1.

claim: The cryo-EM map of caspase-cleaved rXKR9 extends to 4.3 Å resolution.
source: The resulting maps, which extend to 3.66 Å for full-length and 4.3 Å for the cleaved protein, were of high quality and allowed in each case the interpretation with an atomic model (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and documented in Table 1.

claim: The entire rXKR9-sybody complex is about 80 Å high.
source: Viewed perpendicular to the membrane, the entire complex is about 80 Å high, and measures 40×35 Å within the membrane plane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure.

claim: The rXKR9-sybody complex measures 40×35 Å within the membrane plane.
source: Viewed perpendicular to the membrane, the entire complex is about 80 Å high, and measures 40×35 Å within the membrane plane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure.

claim: rXKR9 extends barely beyond the membrane boundary on the extracellular side.
source: On the extracellular side, rXKR9 extends barely beyond the membrane boundary and does not contain any glycosylation sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure.

claim: rXKR9 does not contain any glycosylation sites.
source: On the extracellular side, rXKR9 extends barely beyond the membrane boundary and does not contain any glycosylation sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure.

claim: Sb1XKR9 buries 1466 Å2 of the combined molecular surface when binding to rXKR9.
source: Sb1XKR9 binds to this region burying 1466 Å2 of the combined molecular surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sybody-protein interaction.

claim: rXKR9 comprises eight membrane-spanning helices (TM1–8).
source: rXKR9 comprises eight membrane-spanning helices (TM1–8), which are connected by short loops on the extracellular and longer loops on the intracellular side (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The membrane-spanning helices of rXKR9 are connected by short loops on the extracellular side and longer loops on the intracellular side.
source: rXKR9 comprises eight membrane-spanning helices (TM1–8), which are connected by short loops on the extracellular and longer loops on the intracellular side (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two intracellular regions of rXKR9 harbor α-helices (IH1 and IH2) that are partly embedded in the membrane.
source: Two particularly long intracellular regions harbor α-helices (IH1 and IH2) that are partly embedded in the membrane, whereas other segments are disordered and protrude into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure.

claim: TM3 was not predicted as a membrane-spanning segment due to its hydrophilic character.
source: Although the number of transmembrane helices concurs with predictions by hydropathy analysis (Krogh et al., 2001), there is some discrepancy with respect to their location. Although seven of the helices were correctly predicted, the highly conserved TM3 was, due to its hydrophilic character, not assigned as membrane-spanning segment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing predictions with the actual structure.

claim: IH2 was incorrectly predicted as a transmembrane segment.
source: Conversely, the sixth predicted segment forms the hydrophobic helix IH2 that only spans the inner membrane leaflet and is connected to TM7 by a re-entrant loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing predictions with the actual structure.

claim: The rXKR9 structure consists of two consecutive domains (ND and CD) with similar general organization.
source: The rXKR9 structure consists of two consecutive domains (the N-terminal domain ND and C-terminal domain CD) with similar general organization containing four membrane-spanning helices each (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: TM3 is kinked in the center of the membrane at a conserved PQL motif.
source: The long hydrophilic transmembrane helix TM3 is kinked in the center of the membrane at a conserved PQL motive, which causes a bending away from the membrane normal on its intracellular part to maximize interactions with IH1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The general architecture of XKR9 closely resembles the recently reported structure of XKR8.
source: The general architecture of XKR9 closely resembles the recently reported structure of XKR8 (Sakuragi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the XKR8 structure.

claim: Two furrow-like structures of appropriate size to harbor a lipid are found at the interface between the two domains of rXKR9.
source: Two furrow-like structures of appropriate size to harbor a lipid are found at the interface between the two domains of rXKR9 on both sides of the molecule and an additional structural feature of similar shape is contained within the C-terminal domain (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A bound lipid molecule was observed in cavity C1 of rXKR9.
source: Its appropriate dimensions are underlined by a bound lipid molecule observed in our structure (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cavity C2 contains residual density indicating the presence of bound phospholipids.
source: As the cavity C1, also C2 contains residual density indicating the presence of bound phospholipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cavity C2 contains a cluster of basic amino acids on its intracellular side that might interact with headgroups of negatively charged lipids.
source: On its intracellular side, outside of the hydrophobic membrane core, this region contains a cluster of basic amino acids, which might interact with the headgroups of negatively charged lipids as evidenced by close-by lipid density (Figure 5—figure supplements 1D and 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1D and 2C.

claim: The generally hydrophobic character of the described cavities renders their suitability as a lipid translocation path ambiguous.
source: In all three cases, the generally hydrophobic character of the described cavities renders their suitability as a lipid translocation path ambiguous (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Part of the cleavable C-terminal peptide binds to an intracellular pocket at the interface between the two domains of rXKR9.
source: In case of rXKR9, part of the cleavable peptide, which is only 16 residues long, binds to an intracellular site that is located in a pocket at the interface between the two domains formed by residues of TM3-5, 8, IH2 and the connecting loop regions (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Eight residues at the very C-terminus of rXKR9 are well-defined in the structure.
source: Features in the density suggest the binding of eight residues at the very C-terminus of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structural features.

claim: The C-terminus of rXKR9 buries 1698 Å2 of the combined molecular surface when bound to the protein.
source: These fold into a single turn of an α-helix followed by an extended region that form complementary interactions with the protein burying 1698 Å2 of the combined molecular surface (Figures 3B and 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the C-terminus interaction.

claim: The binding of the C-terminus to rXKR9 is predominantly hydrophobic at its core but involves coulombic interactions at the periphery.
source: The binding is predominantly hydrophobic at its core but involves coulombic interactions at the periphery (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the cleaved rXKR9 structure, the density of the C-terminus is absent.
source: In the data of the cleaved rXKR9, the density of the C-terminus is absent, exposing the hydrophobic cleft to the cytoplasm (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The truncated rXKR9 protein has not changed its conformation significantly compared to full-length, with an RMSD of 0.72 Å.
source: Apart from smaller changes in the intracellular loop regions, the truncated protein has not changed its conformation, which is illustrated in the low RMSD of 0.72 Å between the two structures (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Larger conformational changes during activation might be prevented by the bound sybody or the absence of an endogenous factor.
source: However, at this stage we do not want to exclude the possibility of larger conformational changes during activation as the observed conformation might be either be stabilized by the bound sybody or the absence of an endogenous factor that has also prohibited lipid scrambling in reconstituted samples (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a caveat about the interpretation of the structures.

claim: The addition of a sybody increasing the complex size to 60 kDa was sufficient to obtain high-quality cryo-EM data for rXKR9.
source: However, the addition of a sybody increasing the complex size to 60 kDa was sufficient to obtain high-quality data and thus could provide a suitable general strategy for the structure determination of small and asymmetric membrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the methodological approach.

claim: The rXKR9 structure shows a novel protein fold consisting of two structurally related repeats of four transmembrane helices each.
source: The rXKR9 structures show a novel protein fold, consisting of two structurally related repeats of four transmembrane helices each, that is presumably shared by the entire family irrespective of the function of its members, which is in many cases still elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the structural findings.

claim: The novel protein fold is presumably shared by the entire XKR family.
source: The rXKR9 structures show a novel protein fold, consisting of two structurally related repeats of four transmembrane helices each, that is presumably shared by the entire family irrespective of the function of its members, which is in many cases still elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the structural data.

claim: The 16-residue-long C-terminal peptide acts as an inhibitor of rXKR9 function.
source: The 16-residue-long peptide thus acts as inhibitor of protein function, whose dissociation from its binding site is a requirement for activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Dissociation of the C-terminal peptide from its binding site is a requirement for activation of rXKR9.
source: The 16-residue-long peptide thus acts as inhibitor of protein function, whose dissociation from its binding site is a requirement for activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: No larger rearrangements of the protein were observed as a consequence of proteolysis in the cleaved rXKR9 structure.
source: Although in our structure of the cleaved rXKR9, we do not observe any larger rearrangements of the protein as a consequence of proteolysis (Figure 6B), such conformational changes could be prevented by the bound sybody or the lack of accessory factors, which might lock the protein in its observed conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Conformational changes could be prevented by the bound sybody or the lack of accessory factors.
source: Although in our structure of the cleaved rXKR9, we do not observe any larger rearrangements of the protein as a consequence of proteolysis (Figure 6B), such conformational changes could be prevented by the bound sybody or the lack of accessory factors, which might lock the protein in its observed conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation for the lack of observed conformational changes.

claim: rXKR9 may require an unknown subunit for activation and lipid transport.
source: For rXKR9, we did neither observe an interaction with basigin, nor did we find any indication for the change of the oligomeric state following caspase cleavage (Figure 1B,D), leaving the possibility that the protein might require an unknown subunit for activation and lipid transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation for the lack of observed activity.

claim: The micelle surrounding rXKR9 does not show clear evidence for distortion.
source: The micelle surrounding the protein does not show clear evidence for distortion, which in fungal TMEM16 scramblases was already manifested in structures determined in detergents (Kalienkova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing rXKR9 to TMEM16 scramblases.

claim: Appropriate cavities at the surface of rXKR9 are generally hydrophobic and do not offer obvious interactions with lipid headgroups.
source: Moreover, appropriate cavities located at the surface of the protein, which contain residual densities of bound lipids, are generally hydrophobic and thus do no offer obvious interactions with the lipid headgroups on their way across the membrane (Figures 2 and 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation from the structural data.

claim: A cluster of acidic residues buried in rXKR9 is strongly conserved within family members assigned as lipid scramblases.
source: A remarkable feature of rXKR9 concerns a cluster of acidic residues buried in the protein, which is strongly conserved within family members that were assigned as lipid scramblases, with TM3 being unusually hydrophilic for a transmembrane helix (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: The role of the buried acidic residues for protein function is currently unknown.
source: The role of these residues for protein function is currently unknown, and it is conceivable that they might contribute to lipid scrambling in an active state of the protein, which is likely not displayed in any of our structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: Charged residues might influence the interaction with polar lipid headgroups even if they remain buried after activation.
source: Due to the low dielectric environment of the membrane, charged residues might influence the interaction with polar lipid headgroups even in case they would remain buried after activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the role of charged residues.

claim: Opsins function as lipid scramblases without containing obvious structural features.
source: In light of the lack of structural evidence for its scramblase function, it is noteworthy that opsins were demonstrated to function as lipid scramblases without containing obvious structural features (Menon et al., 2011; Morra et al., 2018) and that the hallmarks described for the fungal scramblases nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014), afTMEM16 (Falzone et al., 2019), or TMEM16K (Bushell et al., 2019) are not displayed in any of the current structures of TMEM16F, whose function as lipid scramblase has been demonstrated in vivo and in vitro (Alvadia et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The hallmarks of fungal TMEM16 scramblases are not displayed in current structures of TMEM16F.
source: In light of the lack of structural evidence for its scramblase function, it is noteworthy that opsins were demonstrated to function as lipid scramblases without containing obvious structural features (Menon et al., 2011; Morra et al., 2018) and that the hallmarks described for the fungal scramblases nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014), afTMEM16 (Falzone et al., 2019), or TMEM16K (Bushell et al., 2019) are not displayed in any of the current structures of TMEM16F, whose function as lipid scramblase has been demonstrated in vivo and in vitro (Alvadia et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The study defined the architecture of a protein that forms a critical part of the machinery leading to PS exposure during programmed cell death.
source: In summary, our study has defined the architecture of a protein that forms a critical part of the machinery leading to the exposure of PS during programmed cell death, which is an essential step leading to the clearance of apoptotic cells (Segawa and Nagata, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the significance of the work.

claim: The study provided initial insight into the activation of XKR family members by caspases.
source: By defining the interaction of the C-terminus, which is removed upon proteolysis, it has also provided initial insight into the activation of family members by caspases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: Activation mechanisms could include conformational changes, dimerization, or binding of an extrinsic interaction partner.
source: These could either include a conformational change that would expose polar patches that are buried in the inactive protein to facilitate lipid flip-flop, dimerization of the protein as suggested for XKR8 and XKR4 (Maruoka et al., 2021; Suzuki et al., 2016), or binding of an extrinsic interaction partner that might contribute part or all of the site responsible for lipid flip-flop.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as possible scenarios for activation.

claim: These activation mechanisms could work in concert to promote the activation of an apoptotic scramblase.
source: These mechanisms could also work in concert to promote the activation of an apoptotic scramblase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about activation mechanisms.
